title: Running Apertus: A Swiss-Made Multimodal LLM
content:
Nowadays in enterprise software engineering there are two primary models of using LLMs and provision them to a fleet of users:
- Commercial Public APIs: Using closed-source models, such as Claude Opus , either directly through vendors like Anthropic or via cloud providers offering managed access to these models, such as Amazon Bedrock and Microsoft Azure AI Foundry. One of the downsides is privacy as companies are sending private information and proprietary code. Other problem the developers are facing is deprecation. The vendors tends to deprecate old models. Such models are used by applications in production that were carefully instrumented and designed to enhance the integration with these models. Forcing developers to go through a complete evaluation, benchmark and Blue/Green deployment process before the model is complete deprecated. There are more concerns. For instance, today it remains unclear whether the judgments done by LLMs are implicitly shaped by geopolitical cues.
- On-Premise Clusters: Deploying open-weights models, such as DeepSeek, Qwen, AMALIA (A Multimodal focused in Portuguese languague and the Portuguese culture), APERTUS (Fully Open Foundation Model for Sovereign AI developed in Switzerland) on internal hardware, such as NVIDIA. These deployments often involved aggressive quantization techniques (e.g., NVFP4) to optimize the underlaying hardware achieving higher throughput and lower latency compared with the base model while keeping all data interaction within the corporate network. There are of course challenges when running self-hosted LLMs. Few of them are: 
  - Computing. You have to own your own GPUs.
  - Knowledge. You have to know how to run an inference-distributed cluster and maintain it.
  - Operability. As everything you own, you have to maintain, monitor and fix when problems appears
I strongly believe we should reduce our dependency on external LLM vendors. They could change their terms, pricing, or policies at any time, potentially putting our workloads and data at risk. We need to achieve AI and LLM sovereignty by maintaining control over our infrastructure, workloads, and data. The internal data is one of the company’s most valuable assets, and we must ensure it remains private and under our control.
In this post, I’ll show you how easy it is to run APERTUS on your own server using the vLLM framework.
Preparation
Before running anything or make any hardware decisions, we need to understand the task at hand. This starts with getting familiar with the characteristics of the LLM we want to run.
Model 
We are going to run the 8B (8-billion-parameter) version of APERTUS. Given that the model uses the BF16 (bfloat16) data type, we will need at least 32 GB of GPU VRAM to run it comfortably.
This is a multilingual model optimized for smaller GPUs. You can learn more about it here.
In order to enable thinking mode, we would need to set --reasoning-parser and --default-chat-template-kwargs.enable_thinking .
As today (October 2026) the Apertus 1.5 release has not been completely merged in the Transformers and vLLM libraries hence we will need to use at least --tool-call-parser as extra Argument when running vLLM. 
Hardware
The accelerator we are going to use is 1 x Nvidia RTX A6000 with 48GB VRAM. Which is enough to run the model we describe above for our own purposes.
LLM Engine
The framework we are going to use to run inference is the very well stablished vLLM.
vLLM comes with a lot of built-in ready optimizations that allow run faster inference servers. Some of its features are:
- Efficient management of attention key and value memory with PagedAttention.
- Continuous batching of incoming requests, chunked prefill, prefix caching
- And more…
Deployment
We are running on an Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS. Let’s install few pre-requisites packages. For the sake of this post we are going to use the vLLM Production-stack which is a reference stack for production deployments.
# Initial OS packages updates
apt-get update
# Clone production-stack repository
git clone https://github.com/vllm-project/production-stack.git
cd production-stack/utils
# install kubectl and verify it is installed
bash install-kubectl.sh
kubectl version --client
# Expected similar output:
Client Version: v1.37.1
Kustomize Version: v5.8.1
### Install helm and verify it is installed
bash install-helm.sh
helm version
# Expected similar output:
version.BuildInfo{Version:"v3.22.1", GitCommit:"d6c1a0e4027caa6abc7892e7ea9f0cda7447baa3", GitTreeState:"clean", GoVersion:"go1.26.9"}
### Instal helm diff plugin
# Source: https://github.com/databus23/helm-diff
helm plugin install https://github.com/databus23/helm-diff
# Expected similar output:
Installed plugin: diff
### Installing Minikube with GPU support
sudo apt remove minikube
bash install-minikube-cluster.sh
#### Verifying GPU Configuration
minikube status
# Expected similar output:
minikube
type: Control Plane
host: Running
kubelet: Running
apiserver: Running
kubeconfig: Configured
kubectl describe nodes | grep -i gpu
# Expected similar output:
  nvidia.com/gpu:     1
# Run a test pod in kubernetes
kubectl run gpu-test --image=nvidia/cuda:12.2.0-runtime-ubuntu22.04 --restart=Never -- nvidia-smi
# Wait for the pod to be in phase: completed, then:
kubectl logs gpu-test
# Expected similar output:
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| NVIDIA-SMI 570.195.03             Driver Version: 570.195.03     CUDA Version: 12.8     |
|-----------------------------------------+------------------------+----------------------+
| GPU  Name                 Persistence-M | Bus-Id          Disp.A | Volatile Uncorr. ECC |
| Fan  Temp   Perf          Pwr:Usage/Cap |           Memory-Usage | GPU-Util  Compute M. |
|                                         |                        |               MIG M. |
|=========================================+========================+======================|
|   0  NVIDIA RTX A6000               On  |   00000000:00:06.0 Off |                  Off |
| 30%   34C    P8             35W /  300W |       1MiB /  49140MiB |      0%      Default |
|                                         |                        |                  N/A |
+-----------------------------------------+------------------------+----------------------+
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Processes:                                                                              |
|  GPU   GI   CI              PID   Type   Process name                        GPU Memory |
|        ID   ID                                                               Usage      |
|=========================================================================================|
|  No running processes found                                                             |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
Easy. At this point we have a Kubernetes cluster using minikube with the Nvidia plugin installed in the cluster and ready to run any GPU workload. Let’s now deploy APERTUS with vLLM.
### Deploy vLLM Instance (model: vllm_apertus_1.5_release)
helm repo add vllm https://vllm-project.github.io/production-stack
# Create a file apertus.yaml with the following (or similar) content
# DO NOT FORGET to set your Hugging Face token in 'hf_token'
servingEngineSpec:
  runtimeClassName: ""
  modelSpec:
  - name: "apertus-8b"
    repository: "ghcr.io/swiss-ai/vllm_apertus_1.5_release"
    tag: "latest-amd64"
    modelURL: "swiss-ai/Apertus-v1.5-8B"
    replicaCount: 1
    requestCPU: 10
    requestMemory: "16Gi"
    requestGPU: 1
    pvcStorage: "50Gi"
    pvcAccessMode:
      - ReadWriteOnce
    vllmConfig:
      enableChunkedPrefill: true
      enablePrefixCaching: true
      maxModelLen: 16384
      extraArgs: ["--gpu-memory-utilization", "0.9", "--enable-auto-tool-choice", "--tool-call-parser", "apertus"]

report.summary: A hands-on guide to self-hosting Switzerland's open Apertus 8B model with vLLM and Kubernetes, framed as a case for AI sovereignty over commercial APIs.
report.background: Enterprises deploying LLMs face a fork in the road: closed commercial APIs (Claude via Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock or Azure AI Foundry) versus self-hosted open-weights models (DeepSeek, Qwen, Portugal's AMALIA, Switzerland's Apertus). The API route outsources operations but sends proprietary code and data to third parties, exposes production systems to sudden model deprecations that force re-benchmarking and Blue/Green redeployments, and raises unanswered questions about geopolitical bias baked into model judgments. The self-hosted route demands owned GPUs, distributed inference expertise and ongoing operability work, but keeps data inside the corporate network and permits aggressive quantization (e.g. NVFP4) for throughput. Apertus, billed as a fully open foundation model for sovereign AI developed in Switzerland, sits squarely in this second camp: a publicly accountable, regionally governed model family that organizations can run on their own hardware without depending on any vendor's terms, pricing or roadmap.
key_points: Apertus 8B is practical on modest hardware: the BF16 model needs roughly 32 GB of VRAM, and the walkthrough uses a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 with 48 GB. It is a multilingual model tuned for smaller GPUs, with an optional thinking mode enabled through vLLM's reasoning-parser and chat-template flags.

The deployment mirrors standard cloud-native ops: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, the vLLM production-stack Helm chart, minikube with GPU support, kubectl and Helm. Verification steps confirm the NVIDIA device plugin is exposing one GPU to the Kubernetes cluster before the model is scheduled.

Configuration is a short YAML manifest: image ghcr.io/swiss-ai/vllm_apertus_1.5_release, model URL swiss-ai/Apertus-v1.5-8B, one replica, one GPU, 50 Gi persistent storage, 16K context, 0.9 GPU memory utilization and chunked prefill plus prefix caching enabled.

A telling rough edge: because Apertus 1.5 is not yet fully merged into Transformers and vLLM, users must pass a model-specific tool-call parser, a reminder that open-weight releases can outpace the libraries that serve them.

The author's motive is sovereignty, not novelty: vendor deprecation cycles force costly re-evaluation of carefully instrumented production apps, and terms, pricing or policy can shift at any time, putting internal data and workloads at risk.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is another data point that regional, publicly funded open-weight models are becoming operationally viable, not just political statements. When an 8B sovereign model runs on a single workstation-class GPU behind a standard Helm chart, the moat around closed API vendors narrows to frontier capability and ecosystem polish rather than deployability. For developers, the barrier to entry is now mostly Kubernetes familiarity plus tolerance for model-specific quirks such as custom tool-call parsers and library lag. For regular users and the businesses serving them, the payoff is data residency and insulation from deprecation churn; the cost is capital expenditure, slower feature cadence and permanent operational ownership, since nobody else is on call when the inference cluster breaks.
report.tools: Follow vLLM and its production-stack Helm chart for the serving layer, minikube or a real Kubernetes cluster with the NVIDIA GPU operator for orchestration, and Hugging Face for the swiss-ai/Apertus-v1.5-8B weights. Watch the Apertus family as it lands fully in Transformers and vLLM, and compare with other sovereign open-weight options such as DeepSeek, Qwen and Portugal's AMALIA when benchmarking self-hosted alternatives.
